---
title: "Did climate change make Black Summer fires more likely in Australia?"
author: "Xuanning Zhang"
date: "2026-10-11"
bibliography: reference.bib
---

The sky turned orange over southeastern Australia in the summer of 2019-20. The "Black Summer" bush fires burned more than 19 million hectares of land, killed 34 people and destroyed around 5900 homes and other buildings. Smoke has blanketed cities like Sydney and Canberra, nearly 80% Aussies said their living has been affected. Perhaps you are one of them. So, is it only a disaster season or caused by human activity? A major international research has confirmed that comparing to 1900s, the climate change has increased the occurrence of dangerous fire weather at least 30%, and probably much more [@vanoldenborgh2021].

## What happened? And what did scientists asked?

In that summer, many people watching this news asked this question, but it is harder to answer than it sounds. A bushfire need ingredients of hot weather, strong winds, dry vegetation and source of ignition like lightning or people. Climate change will not light fires,and there has not fire season can be blamed on single one factor. So scientists asked another question: how much more the climate change increased the probability of hot, dry and windy weather that let the fire spread so far? You can even imagine that every road could happening car accident, but wet road will strongly increase the probability.

To find out, a team of international scientists has compared the likelihood of weather in "Black Summer" from 2019-20 to that around 1900. They used two kinds evidence: the Australian weather records from 1910 and computer models of the climate, which can simulate the weather condition overtime. These evidences let scientists count out the frequency of extreme weather in different periods. The team has divided the research inyo three aspects: drought, extreme heat and overall fire weather.

## Explain the Evidences

The climate records for fire weather came from ERA5, which combines the previous climate observations with climate model since 1979. Scientists used the Fire Weather Index (FWI) to measure how dangerous the weather is, it could be seen as a danger score which combines the temperature, humidity, wind and rainfall into one value, as higher FWI, as bushfire is easier to start and spread. The research focus on most dangerous week of each fire season, as there has more land burned in southeastern Australia with higher FWI, thus it is a useful measurement index.

These three factors reflect different situations (@tbl-finding). Extreme heat shows a clear relationship, that human-caused climate change has increased the probability of hot week twice. The climate record shows if the similar extreme heat happen around 1900, the temperature of same heat wave will have 1 to 2 °C lower. Drought is different because the team did not find a clear relationship in human-caused extreme rainfall shortage, but it does not mean there has no effect on drought by climate change, but did not detect one. The drought in 2019 was mainly drove by two climate modes: the Indian Ocean Dipole and the Southern Annular Mode, both of them explained roughly one-third of the rain fall deficit from July to December in 2019. While all factors are considered in FWI, the result is obvious: extreme weather like "Black Summer" have at least 30% higher than around 1900 which mainly due to rise in extreme heat.


::: {#tbl-finding .cell tbl-cap='How climate change affected three factors in Black Summer\'s weather comparing to around 1900'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Factor                     |Findings                    |Explanation                                                               |
|:--------------------------|:---------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Extreme heat               |At least twice as likely    |Heat wave in 2019 Dec will been 1-2 °C cooler if it happen in around 1900 |
|Extreme rainfall shortages |No human-caused trend found |Can't reject it, the research did not detect a trend in the drought       |
|Extreme fire weather       |At least 30% more likely    |Mainly because extreme heat became more likely                            |


:::
:::


According to ERA5 climate records, the probability of fire weather like "Black Summer" is at least four times higher than around 1900 (@fig-fire-risk). The model also suggest that in a world 2°C warmer than pre-industrial level, the disaster climate will be at least four times than the beginning of 20th century. Also, the risk has already risen and predicted to keep rising.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The extreme fire weather as Black Summer is now more likely than around 1900. Plot shows the minimum increase reported by research.](black_summer_files/figure-html/fig-fire-risk-1.png){#fig-fire-risk width=672}
:::
:::



These data come with an important limitation, the climate model tend to underestimate how quickly extreme heat has increased, thus the actual increased risk could be larger than expectation. Furthermore, the climate data only cover the time after 1979, but there was a drying trend in this period and may make the "four times" too high, the 2°C projection is also based on two models. That is why we should focus on cautious lower bounds rather than the most dramatic numbers.

## Not just a bad summer

Back to our question: Did climate change caused Black Summer? Climate change did not light the fires. The evidence shows human-caused climate change increased the probability of dangerous fire weather mainly because it make extreme heat more frequent. The likelihood of extreme heat week in December 2019 has increase at least twice as likely as that around 1900 and fire weather like 2019-20 has increased at least 30%, and this risk is still increasing. The research did not find a clear trend of human-caused rain fall deficits and drought is still an open question.

What does this mean for you? If you living in southeastern Australia, the fire weather like Black Summer is not as rare as a century ago, but more common due to global warming. Here are few simple steps: Check the danger rating on hot days, cleaning dry leaves and plants near your house on time and set a bushfire plan. *No one can stop every fire, but better understanding of risk can help us be ready for the next Black Summer*.
